title: Bjarke Alexander Larson - Corrupted Databases - Building a Repeatable Logic Puzzle in a Discord Bot
speaker: Bjarke Alexander Larsen
summary: Bjarke Alexander Larsen describes the procedurally generated database puzzle in Telegrams from the Quiet Train, a communal shipping-management narrative game played over weeks through a Discord bot. Players must find a recipient's true name and address by correlating 13 deliberately corrupted databases generated from a simulated ground truth. He explains why an early five-database version was boring, how varied database quirks and varied starting information give each puzzle a unique path and a difficulty signal, and how he handled unsolvable puzzles by giving players a narratively justified paid way out instead of guaranteeing solvability.

insights.claim: Telegrams from the Quiet Train builds a repeatable logic puzzle by deriving several corrupted databases from a hidden ground truth and asking players to correlate them to find the true answer.
insights.detail: Lore says a distorting force corrupted all stored text, so 13 databases each give a different version of the truth (e.g. four possible addresses for one name). Players start from a trusted recipient ID and cross-reference databases, accepting an answer once several sources agree; Larsen walks through finding an address that appears in both the voting registry and the commuting registry and then confirming it with two more databases.
insights.quote: you correlate multiple databases to find the info that is most likely to be true based on what's based on the correlations that you find

insights.claim: The database puzzle in Telegrams from the Quiet Train grew out of data the game already needed, giving players something to do during real-time waits while the train moves.
insights.detail: The game is played over weeks with trains taking real days to arrive, and all core activities happened while the train was stationary. Larsen already had a database of people and addresses for the shipping system and looked for a way to turn it into an activity.
insights.quote: I already had a database of people and locations because I needed that for the shipping management aspect of the game

insights.claim: The ground truth for the corrupted databases is generated by simulating 50 to 100 years of people moving house, then applying naive random corruptions to make several wrong versions.
insights.detail: Each person gets an initial address and a simulated history of moves, with the newest address being current. Corrupted copies randomly add, replace, remove and shuffle addresses, done several times to produce databases that are wrong in different ways.
insights.quote: I randomly added new addresses. I randomly replaced some of them. I randomly removed some of them and I shuffled them around

insights.claim: With only five similar databases, the puzzle collapsed into a dominant strategy of querying everything and picking the most frequent answer, which playtesters found boring.
insights.detail: All five databases mapped name to address or address to name, so it was easy to query all of them and see the answer by frequency. Larsen says this quickly became the optimal play pattern and was not interesting.
insights.quote: it was relatively simple to just query all five and then immediately see the answer based on which uh which which value appeared the most frequently

insights.claim: Making each database map different fields and corrupting each in its own characteristic way lets players learn the 'texture' of each source and makes brute-force querying less attractive.
insights.detail: Larsen expanded to 13 databases, each with different inputs and outputs (names to jobs, work address to home addresses, etc.). Some only add wrong answers so the right one is always present, others shuffle more or are more corrupted, so players learn over time how trustworthy and useful each is.
insights.quote: hopefully players over time like learn the textures of what kind of answers a database tends to give um and how useful they are

insights.claim: Varying which pieces of information the player starts with gives each puzzle instance a unique path through the web of databases, keeping repeated puzzles fresh.
insights.detail: Instead of always starting from a name, each order starts with an ID revealing a varying subset of information. Starting with name and job leads through different databases than starting with home address and district, which Larsen calls key to making instances feel unique over a long-running game.
insights.quote: it gives each version each instance of the puzzle a unique path through the databases

insights.claim: The amount of information revealed up front serves as a difficulty measure that is shown to players so they can opt into harder or easier puzzles.
insights.detail: Giving four of five needed facts makes an easy puzzle; giving two makes a hard one. When choosing an order, the game indicates how corrupted the entry is so players pick their difficulty.
insights.quote: people pick an order to sort of indicate, hey, this is a pretty corrupted database entry. You're going to have a harder time with this one

insights.claim: Playtesting showed naive random corruption rarely produced truly unsolvable puzzles, because many crisscrossing databases left probable answers even when a puzzle looked impossible.
insights.detail: Larsen had guaranteed solvability in the simple version by checking that the right answer appeared at least twice, but skipped the check in the complex version and playtested. The layered databases meant logical inference usually found a probable answer.
insights.quote: even puzzles that looked pretty impossible from the outset actually often had probable answers

insights.claim: A puzzle that feels impossible makes players give up just as if it were impossible, so the design problem is the player's perception, not only actual solvability.
insights.detail: Larsen found the real issue was players perceiving puzzles as impossible and quitting, a feel-bad moment, rather than how many puzzles were truly unsolvable.
insights.quote: feeling like it's impossible and it being impossible then often becomes the same thing

insights.claim: Instead of guaranteeing solvability, Telegrams from the Quiet Train lets players report a puzzle as impossible and pay a narratively justified fee to have another company solve it.
insights.detail: Contracting out the corruption costs part of the reward but feels much better than being stuck, fits the fiction, and doubles as an opt-out for players who don't want to do the puzzles at all. It worked so well it was expanded into a global shared database where players report which entries are corrupted.
insights.quote: rather than solving uh the the the core underlying thing I gave uh uh a players an out

insights.claim: You can sometimes get away with unchecked randomness in generated puzzles if players have a good way of dealing with the bad outcomes.
insights.detail: Larsen's conclusion pairs this with the point that database puzzles are more fun with varied entry points requiring different traversals each time.
insights.quote: you can sometimes get away with totally randomness if players have a good way of feeling of of dealing with it
